segments.say: Now picture the old footbridge, painted dark green, arching gently over the slow river. It's narrow, just wide enough for two people to pass. Its iron rail is cool and smooth, worn by more than a hundred years of hands, and tonight it's covered in a fine layer of frost that sparkles softly under the lamps at each end.

Picture walking slowly onto the bridge, and stopping halfway across, the way Elena did. Lean gently on the rail. Look down at the dark water sliding by beneath you, carrying the moonlight with it. The bridge holds you safely. It has held so many people, on so many nights. It's very good at holding.

Underneath the bridge, the river keeps moving, slowly and steadily, always on its way somewhere else. The water you see now will soon be far downstream, and new water will take its place. Your thoughts can be like that too. Let each one flow past, and on, and away, while you stay here, still and quiet, on the bridge.

Notice your hands. Perhaps they're resting by your sides, or on the covers. Let them feel warm, and heavy, and completely relaxed. Let your fingers uncurl, softly. Imagine the cool iron rail of the bridge under them, and the warmth of your hands slowly spreading into it, until the rail and your hands are both just pleasantly warm.

Picture the two lamps, one at each end of the bridge, glowing softly like two friends who've agreed to keep watch, one on each bank, all night long. Between them, the bridge rests in a gentle half-light. And you, halfway across, are held safely between the two lights, with the river murmuring beneath.

Picture a single ripple on the water below, perhaps from a fish, or a falling leaf. It spreads out slowly in a widening ring, bigger and bigger and fainter and fainter, until it melts away into the calm surface and is gone. Let any last thought you're holding spread out like that ripple, wider and softer, until it melts away too.

The moon is higher now, and its light makes a long silver path across the river, from the far bank almost to your feet. It shimmers softly as the water moves. You don't need to walk on it. You can just look at it, and let it lead your thoughts away, gently, across the water, into the quiet dark.

If you look down from the bridge in just the right place, where the water is calmest, you can see the stars reflected in the river. Little points of light, trembling very gently on the dark surface. Stars above you, and stars below you, and you resting quietly in between, on the old green bridge.

Take a slow breath here, on the bridge. In, all the way, filling up gently like the river after rain. And out, all the way, like the water flowing away downstream. And another. In, slowly. And out, slowly. Each breath a little deeper, a little softer, a little more like sleep.

Listen to the night around the bridge. There's the soft murmur of the water. Maybe, far away, a dog barks once and is quiet again. Maybe a car passes on a distant road and fades into silence. And then there's almost nothing at all. Just a deep, soft hush, like the inside of a snowfall.

When you're ready, picture yourself pushing off gently from the rail and carrying on across the bridge. Step by step, slowly. The boards are firm under your feet. The river murmurs below. And with each step, you're leaving the day a little further behind you, on the other bank, where it can't reach you any more.

On the far side of the bridge, a little path leads up into the park. The grass on either side is white with frost, and the trees are bare and silver. The path is lit by just a few soft lamps, far apart, so that most of it lies in a gentle, comfortable darkness. You walk into it, slowly, and it feels like walking into sleep.

Picture the frosted grass, each blade coated in tiny crystals of ice, all standing perfectly still. In the morning, when the sun comes up, it will sparkle and melt. But for now it rests, white and quiet, a soft carpet spread out under the trees, all the way across the park, as far as you can see in the dark.

If your eyes are still open, you might let them close now, gently. And if they're already closed, let them rest even more deeply, the muscles around them softening, the eyelids growing heavy. There's nothing you need to see. The park is there, in your mind, as calm and as quiet as you'd like it to be.

Up ahead, under a single soft lamp, the old oak tree stands with its great bare branches spreading out against the stars. And beneath it, the wooden bench, waiting, just as Elena found it. Picture walking slowly towards it, across the frosted grass, one soft, unhurried step at a time.
